articles.description: In other news, ACME Group has approved a $3.6 billion green ammonia project in India, while researchers in Chile have assessed hydrogen production from curtailed renewable power. Qair has inaugurated a hydrogen plant in France, Plug Power has launched a utility-scale electrolyzer offering, and Protium has advanced two UK hydrogen projects.
paragraphs: Qair has inaugurated its Hyd’Occ renewable hydrogen production facility in Occitanie, France. The 20 MW plant is supported by a regional network of hydrogen refueling stations forming part of the European H2 Corridor. Qair opened its first hydrogen refueling stations in Béziers and Narbonne in spring 2026. A second development phase will double the plant’s installed capacity to 40 MW, increasing annual hydrogen production capacity to 5,400 tons. Total investment amounts to €130 million.

Plug Power has launched GenEco Scale, an integrated electrolyzer plant offering for utility-scale hydrogen production. Arcadia eFuels has selected the system for a 280 MW hydrogen facility at its Project ARC development in Texas. Plug Power said it has completed the project’s technical evaluation and front-end engineering design (FEED) study. Once operational, the facility is expected to support production of approximately 23.2 million gallons of electro-sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF) annually. Plug Power previously signed a 280 MW electrolyzer supply agreement with Arcadia eFuels for a separate project in Denmark.

Protium has completed due diligence for two green hydrogen projects under the UK government’s second Hydrogen Allocation Round (HAR2). The South Tees Net Zero project in northern England and the South Wales Net Zero project have both advanced to the Invitation to Offer stage. The 70 MW South Tees facility is designed to produce up to 11,000 tons of green hydrogen annually, equivalent to about 433 GWh, for industrial consumers in Teesside. The projects will now progress toward Low Carbon Hydrogen Agreements, which provide revenue support to reduce investment risks. Protium is also developing other UK hydrogen projects, including a 15 MW electrolyzer project that secured support under the first Hydrogen Allocation Round.

articles.title: Proper Voltage, Unigrid unveil sodium-ion storage solution for data centers
articles.description: The Salt Vault High Power cabinet aims to deliver some of the benefits of sodium-ion chemistries including the concept that rapid and repeated power transients may not degrade sodium-ion batteries as fast as lithium and lead-acid.
paragraphs: California-based duo Proper Voltage and Unigrid have teamed up to pair voltage-control electronics with sodium-chromium oxide cells to create a 73.1 kWh backup cabinet aimed at delivering power to data centers.

Battery integration firm Proper Voltage announced that it has launched Salt Vault, an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery cabinet built around sodium-ion cells from San Diego-based Unigrid. Commercial deliveries to unnamed early-adopter data center and critical infrastructure operators are scheduled to begin in April 2027.
The system combines Proper Voltage’s software that it calls its battery operating system (bOS) with Unigrid’s sodium-chromium oxide (NCO) chemistry.

According to Proper Voltage’s product specifications, the Salt Vault High Power cabinet delivers 73.1 kWh of capacity and 333 kW of power output at a nominal 522 VDC, rated for 10,000 cycles. It operates across a discharge temperature range of -20 C to 40 C and a charge range of 0 C to 40 C. A single module in the cabinet is 6.1 kWh.

The two companies are targeting a specific operational problem in AI data centers, where training and inference clusters swing from idle to peak load in milliseconds. Those repeated power transients may accelerate degradation in conventional lead-acid and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) backup batteries.

Proper Voltage says its software-defined voltage control as part of its bOS regulates output across the full state of charge, allowing the sodium-ion cabinet to drop into existing UPS architectures without inverter redesigns. It can also adapt to 800 V racks, as the industry scales towards that voltage level.

“Performance is what drives the best models, and the battery behind them must be resilient and adaptive across every one of those demands,” said Charlie Welch, CEO of Proper Voltage. Unigrid CEO Darren Tan said the NCO chemistry is built for high-rate pulse power and thermal stability under heavy cycling.
The launch adds to a growing push by sodium-ion developers into AI infrastructure, where fire safety and high-rate discharge may matter more than energy density.
Earlier this year, Energy Vault locked in 1.5 GWh of Peak Energy’s sodium-ion systems for its AI data center portfolio.
And, less happily, ESS Tech introduced a modular sodium-ion platform for the same market in July, before it went out of business in November.

articles.title: Can a developer turn data centers’ reputation around?
articles.description: A conversation with Charley Daitch and JD Lambert of Rowan.
paragraphs: When people push for better data centers, they picture hyperscalers — Amazon, say, or Meta. But the company that buys the land, lines up the power, and deals with the county commission is often a developer nobody’s heard of. So who can actually deliver on sustainability? Who can be held to it? I talk with Charley Daitch and JD Lambert of Rowan, a self-described sustainable developer, about what developers control, what they leave to tenants and utilities, and whether the industry’s promises belong in law.

When people think of data centers, they generally imagine the big tech companies like Google, Meta, and Amazon building them. But the fact is, most of those facilities are built by companies you’ve never heard of, developers who do the work of finding the land, lining up the power, dealing with the county commission, and constructing the shell. They rent those shells out to tech companies.

It’s the developers that most often face the local fights over noise, water, power bills, and tax breaks. So it’s worth asking, in terms of sustainability, what a developer can control, and what it can’t.

Rowan Digital Infrastructure is one of the bigger players in that layer — it has roughly two gigawatts under construction in Maryland, Texas, and Oregon. It markets itself as the sustainable, community-first developer. It recently put out a “community guarantee” with pledges on transparency, water, and ratepayer costs.

But pledges are only pledges. I’m curious which of these commitments a developer can actually keep, given that the tenant often controls things like backup generation and load behavior, and what penalties, if any, there are for failing to do so.

So I’m talking today with Rowan’s CEO, Charley Daitch, who came over from running energy and water strategy at AWS, and JD Lambert, Rowan’s director of sustainable practices. We’re going to get into Texas, Maryland, water, and what towns ought to be demanding before they say yes. Let’s do this.
David Roberts: All right, let’s do this. With no further ado, Charley Daitch, JD Lambert, welcome to Volts. Thank you so much for coming.

David Roberts: All right. So Charley, let’s start with you just as a little background here. As I said, I think most people imagine the tech companies that are doing the AI, that are doing the computing, they sort of imagine them building the data centers, but that’s not really how it works. So maybe just explain: what does a developer do? What does Rowan do? Which parts of a data center campus do you build and own and run versus what the tenant owns and runs, and who’s responsible for what?

Charley Daitch: Yeah. There’s no one model, David, but let me speak to it generally, and then we can speak to where some of the nuances are as well. So the way that Rowan creates value for our customers is that we go out and we find where is there power available on the electric grid, where is there land and communities that are gonna be receptive, and also, you know, how will this site ultimately fit into the broader compute architecture of our hyperscale customers? We buy that land, we bring it through entitlements, we work with utility providers, we work really closely with communities to make sure that our development fits within their plans as well.

articles.title: Chinese PV Industry Brief: China Three Gorges opens 5.24 GW solar module tender
articles.description: China Three Gorges has opened bidding for 5.24 GW of solar modules for 2027, while TCL Zhonghuan plans to increase its stake in a semiconductor subsidiary. In other news, Longi has secured a module supply deal in Australia, and China is stepping up efforts to recycle retired PV panels.
paragraphs: China’s National Energy Administration (NEA) said the country added 110.329 GW of grid-connected solar capacity in the first nine months of 2026, including 45.80 GW of utility-scale PV and 64.52 GW of distributed solar, of which 33.46 GW came from residential installations. Cumulative grid-connected solar capacity reached 1.31 TW at the end of September, with Jiangsu, Henan and Yunnan recording the largest additions. The figures follow an earlier NEA report showing a sharp year-on-year decline in solar installations.

China’s Ministry of Commerce (Mofcom), together with eight other government agencies, has issued guidelines to strengthen the country’s recycling system, identifying retired PV modules, power batteries and wind turbine blades as priority areas. The policy encourages market-based cooperation between state-owned power companies and recycling enterprises, alongside the expansion of collection networks and recycling facilities. Authorities also plan to develop specific regulations for the recycling and disposal of decommissioned PV modules. China previously outlined plans to establish a recycling system for retired solar panels and wind turbines.

TCL Zhonghuan has proposed acquiring an additional 65.80% stake in Zhonghuan Leading Semiconductor Technology through a share issuance, increasing its ownership from 32.72% to 98.52% upon completion. At a media briefing, the company reaffirmed solar and semiconductor materials as its two core businesses. It said its solar operations would focus on scaling back-contact (BC) technology and expanding internationally, with no plans for significant new wafer manufacturing capacity in the near term. TCL Zhonghuan previously announced plans to convert 20 GW of TOPCon cell capacity to BC technology.

Longi has signed an agreement to supply 176 MW of Hi-MO 9 back-contact modules for the Muswellbrook solar-plus-storage project in New South Wales, Australia. Developed by OX2 at a rehabilitated former coal mine, the project will include a 100 MWh battery energy storage system. Grid connection is expected in 2028, with annual solar generation estimated at 347 GWh. The project forms part of a broader renewable energy development at the former Muswellbrook coal mine.

JA Solar has launched an integrated solar-and-storage ecosystem in Chengdu, China, combining PV generation, battery storage, energy management and unified operations and maintenance services. The company claims the solution could improve system efficiency by 2% to 3%, cut installation and commissioning times by 20% to 30%, and reduce lifecycle project management costs by approximately 30% compared with systems assembled from separately supplied equipment. The projected benefits have not yet been independently verified through operational data. JA Solar previously announced a broader strategy covering solar, storage and integrated energy services.

Arctech has secured a tracker supply contract for the 500 MW Al Kamil I solar project in Oman. The Chinese manufacturer will supply its SkyLine II tracking system, which uses multi-point parallel-drive technology and is designed to withstand wind speeds exceeding 56 meters per second. Arctech said the system is engineered to improve structural stability and long-term reliability in high-wind desert environments. The company previously secured tracker supply agreements for a 2.1 GW solar project in the United Arab Emirates.

articles.title: Vietnam sets rooftop solar monitoring and control acceptance procedure
articles.description: Vietnam's state-owned utility has introduced a formal acceptance testing procedure for rooftop solar systems connected to its monitoring and control systems.
paragraphs: Vietnam’s state-owned national power utility Vietnam Electricity (EVN) has introduced new technical requirements and acceptance procedures for rooftop solar installations that export surplus electricity to the grid.

Decision No. 1382/QĐ-EVN, issued on November 18, sets out technical specifications and a process for testing and accepting rooftop solar installations connected to EVN’s monitoring, data-collection and control systems. It replaces Decision No. 378/QĐ-EVN, issued on Mar. 12, 2025, and takes effect immediately.
The requirements cover rooftop solar systems designed for self-consumption that export surplus electricity to the grid and fall within the electricity company’s monitoring and control remit.
Under the specifications, installations must transmit operational data to the electricity company’s monitoring system, with inverter output updated at intervals of no more than five minutes.
Systems must also be capable of both receiving and executing remote commands to limit exported power, as well as automatically adjusting inverter output to comply with instructions from the utility.

The acceptance testing procedure includes documentation reviews, site inspections, communications testing and verification of monitoring and control signals. Utilities must also test a system’s ability to reduce exports in response to power limitation commands and check its behaviour during communications outages and faults before issuing any acceptance documentation.

EVN says system owners are responsible for installing compatible monitoring, metering and communications equipment, providing technical documentation and coordinating with utilities during testing. Electricity companies are responsible for providing connection and communications configurations, verifying cybersecurity and monitoring functionality and conducting the acceptance tests.

The decision comes as Vietnam looks to accelerate rooftop solar deployment. The Vietnamese government ordered provinces to speed up rooftop solar support policies in September. Last month, it called on provincial and municipal authorities to introduce these policies by the end of the year.

A Ministry of Industry and Trade publication released in September also outlined plans to link distributed rooftop solar, behind-the-meter battery energy storage systems and electric vehicles into flexible grid assets, moving away from basic time-of-use tariffs.

Vietnam’s solar capacity surpassed 19 GW by the end of 2025, with around 586 MW of solar added last year. The country had more than 11.45 GW of rooftop solar capacity across 134,410 installations as of the end of August 2026, according to figures from EVN.

articles.title: High pressure drives irradiance gains across South East Asia as Sichuan misses out
articles.description: In a new weekly update for pv magazine, Solcast, a DNV company, reports that October 2026 saw solar irradiance exceed average levels by over 20% across southern China and Southeast Asia, driven by strong El Niño conditions, persistent high pressure, and reduced cloud cover. However, cloudiness in Sichuan and Chongqing, cold fronts, Typhoon Champi, and wildfire haze in Indonesia reduced solar irradiance in some areas.
paragraphs: October 2026 brought unusually sunny conditions across much of southern China and mainland South East Asia, with irradiance 20%+ above average in the strongest-affected areas, according to analysis using the Solcast API. Persistent high pressure over South East Asia and the South China Sea, alongside a very strong El Niño, suppressed rainfall and cloud. Sichuan and Chongqing missed much of the irradiance boost, while repeated cold fronts and Typhoon Champi interrupted the broader pattern farther north and east.

The strongest positive irradiance anomalies stretched across Yunnan, Guangxi, Guangdong and Hainan, through northern Indochina and into the Philippines. Rainfall was up to 6 millimeters per day below average across much of the same region, helping keep skies clearer. October rainfall in the southern southwest was more than 50% below normal, with drought persisting in Yunnan, southwest Guizhou and southern Guangxi. Southern and central China were also more than 1.5 C warmer than average. Hong Kong recorded its warmest October, with a mean temperature of 27.6 C. A weaker northeast monsoon and persistent high pressure helped limit the usual influx of moisture and cloud, reinforcing the sunnier pattern during a very strong El Niño.

Sichuan and Chongqing were a notable exception. While surrounding regions recorded positive irradiance anomalies, the basin saw slightly below-average irradiance for October. More easterly winds than usual and lower pressure over the Sichuan Basin helped keep cloud concentrated over the region, with the surrounding terrain and anomalously high pressure limiting its dispersal. The additional cloud coincided with neutral to slightly above-average rainfall in October, in contrast with the drier conditions surrounding the basin and farther south.

Farther north and east, repeated cold-air outbreaks brought periods of increased cloud and precipitation, interrupting the otherwise favourable irradiance conditions. China experienced six cold-air outbreaks during October, 2.4 more than average. These brought rain and snow across parts of northern and eastern China, with eastern Hebei and most of Beijing receiving 50–100 mm of precipitation from 15–23 October.

Typhoon Champi provided another interruption to the broader pattern. The storm formed on 11 October and reached winds near 215 km/h, affecting Taiwan, Japan and China. Cloud and rainfall associated with the system reduced irradiance as it moved through the region, with 62,400 people evacuated in Shanghai due to the conditions. October was particularly active for tropical weather overall, with eight tropical cyclones across the South China Sea and western North Pacific during the month.

Farther south, Sumatra and Kalimantan recorded below-average irradiance despite substantial rainfall deficits. Indonesia had recorded more than 1.06 million fire hotspots by 14 October, with widespread smoke and haze reducing incoming sunlight despite the otherwise dry conditions. Aerosol optical depth shows where the heaviest concentrations of smoke and haze occurred during the month.

articles.title: JinkoSolar claims 35.24% efficiency for perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell
articles.description: The result was confirmed by the Shanghai Institute of Microsystem and Information Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
paragraphs: Chinese solar module manufacturer JinkoSolar has announced that it has achieved a power conversion efficiency of 35.24% for a perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell.

The company said the result was certified by the Shanghai Institute of Microsystem and Information Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS). JinkoSolar previously achieved an efficiency of 34.82% with the same cell configuration.

“This efficiency breakthrough was made possible by multiple core technological innovations, including selective passivation technology for textured silicon surfaces in N-type TOPCon, a perovskite multi-component crystallization synchronization control strategy, and nanoscale interface passivation materials and light-management enhancement technologies,” the company said in a statement, adding that the efficiency improvement was achieved over five months.
The company did not disclose further technical details about the cell or the efficiency improvement.

The current world record for perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell efficiency is held by Chinese manufacturer Longi, which achieved 35.5% efficiency in July 2026. The result, obtained with a two-terminal tandem cell, was independently certified by the European Solar Test Installation (ESTI). It surpassed Longi’s previous certified record of 34.85%, announced in April 2025.

Longi also recently reported an efficiency of 35.31% for a tandem cell incorporating specially designed self-assembled molecules. Longi previously achieved a certified efficiency of 34.85% in April 2025 and an efficiency of 34.3% for a large-area tandem cell measuring 261 cm².

In January 2026, Chinese module maker Trinasolar achieved 32.6% efficiency for a large-area tandem cell developed with Huairou Laboratory, with the result certified by Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (Fraunhofer ISE).

articles.title: It’s official: 2026 is the year of lost solar in North Carolina
articles.description: State regulators have doubled down on a spring decision to cancel 2026 bids for Duke Energy solar contracts, amounting to a gigawatt’s worth of missing…
paragraphs: This spring, when North Carolina’s top utility regulator abruptly canceled bidding for new Duke Energy large solar contracts for 2026, critics filed an array of legal motions in protest, calling the unilateral order from the chair of the Utilities Commission ​ “ arbitrary and capricious” — and likely illegal.

But as the cases dragged on through the summer and fall, the clean energy industry and its advocates began to worry they had lost by default: The year was almost over, leaving no time for Duke to solicit proposals for new solar projects.

Now, the loss is official. On Monday, as part of its decision approving Duke’s long-term carbon reduction plan, the commission ruled that some solar megawatts the company had planned to procure in 2026 should be punted to future years. On Tuesday, the panel rejected pleas from a clean energy trade group and a coalition of nonprofits that it ​ “ reconsider” its spring order.

The rulings mean Duke will contract for an additional 2. 3 gigawatts of solar to come online by 2034, the company says, bringing the total added under a 2021 state law to about 6. 4 GW. That figure reflects over a gigawatt of solar foregone this year alone.

“ We just completely skipped a year of solar procurement in the state,” said Nick Jimenez, senior attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, which appealed the spring order on behalf of the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, Vote Solar, and the Sierra Club. ​ “ That’s a huge missed opportunity in terms of bringing low-cost generation online in North Carolina.”

Jimenez and other advocates see the meager utility-scale solar investment as one among many flaws in Duke’s latest carbon reduction plan, a document required every two years to chart its course to zero carbon by 2050. The blueprint includes one of the largest natural gas buildouts in the U.S. and a delay in the retirement of costly coal plants.

The 2026 solar backsliding comes in part because of punishing tariffs and expiring tax credits pushed through by President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans; in their orders, commissioners noted that both policies make the renewable energy resource more expensive for customers. They also said there was a ​ “ reduced near-term need for solar” after the Republican-led state legislature last year repealed a requirement that Duke cut its carbon pollution by 70 % by 2030.

Playing catch-up in future years is certainly possible, solar industry leaders say, but it will be more expensive for North Carolina consumers, since continued inflation and tariff pressures make it likely that solar prices will rise after 2026.

“ We can no longer expect that the price of solar is going to go down every year,” said Carson Harkrader, a solar developer and chair of the Carolinas Clean Energy Business Association, the trade group that challenged the spring cancellation. ​ “ So when solar procurements are pushed out, we lose the opportunity to lock in our prices as early as possible and deliver lower-priced solar energy for ratepayers.”

articles.title: It’s another banner year for batteries in the US
articles.description: Through the first nine months of this year, nearly a dozen states had already beat their annual installation records for energy storage.
paragraphs: See more from Canary Media’s ​ “ Chart of the Week” column. Batteries are booming in America.

Over the first nine months of this year, the U.S. installed 20 % more battery storage capacity than it did in the same period last year, according to a new report by the Solar Energy Industries Association and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Most of that capacity is from utility-scale installations, though it includes residential and commercial installations, too.

In the last decade, batteries have gotten exponentially cheaper and have rapidly become one of the most important grid technologies. The systems are relatively speedy to install, and their ability to store inexpensive surplus power for later has captivated utilities, data center developers, and households alike.

Even without the final three months of data for 2026, 11 states have already seen battery installations reach record levels this year: Alabama, Colorado, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Massachusetts, Michigan, Mississippi, Montana, Utah, and Virginia.

The bad news is that the report predicts residential installations will drop 8 % this year compared to 2025. That sector took a hit after the federal government ripped away incentives for home energy storage at the end of last year, though SEIA and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence say business is recovering faster than expected.

Despite the residential dip, the report authors expect overall battery capacity additions in 2026 to surpass last year’s figures by 26 %. It’s a testament to the tech’s broad appeal — and a bright spot for the energy transition, which will rely on abundant storage to spread wind and solar power through all hours of the day.

articles.title: Mexico’s solar capacity could reach 43.8 GW by 2035
articles.description: GlobalData has raised its solar growth forecast for Mexico by 6 GW, citing a growing pipeline of renewable energy projects. However, grid congestion, transmission constraints and regulatory uncertainty could slow deployment.
paragraphs: Mexico’s installed solar capacity is expected to increase from 13.7 GW in 2025 to 43.8 GW by 2035, according to the latest report on the Mexican electricity market by research and consultancy firm GlobalData. The firm forecasts that renewables will account for 42.3% of the country’s total installed power capacity by 2035, up from 22.9% in 2025.
The latest projection represents an upward revision of 6 GW from GlobalData’s December 2025 forecast, which put Mexico’s installed solar capacity at 37.8 GW by 2035.

The Mexico Power Market Trends and Analysis by Capacity, Generation, Transmission, Distribution, Regulations, Key Players and Forecast to 2035 report projects that Mexico’s total installed power capacity will increase from 104.2 GW in 2025 to 156 GW in 2035, representing a compound annual growth rate of 4.1%. Over the same period, natural gas-fired generation capacity is expected to rise from 53.4 GW to 64.8 GW.

Despite the expansion of renewables, GlobalData expects thermal power plants to continue accounting for nearly 60% of Mexico’s electricity generation in 2035, while the share of renewables in the generation mix is projected to increase from 14.5% to 31.9%. The consultancy also forecasts that electricity consumption will rise from 328.5 TWh in 2025 to 423.2 TWh in 2035, driven by industrial nearshoring, the expansion of data centers, and growing demand for air conditioning.

Attaurrahman Ojindaram Saibasan, a power sector analyst at GlobalData, said the 2025 Electricity Sector Law and the binding nature of the 2025-2039 Electricity Sector Development Plan (PLADESE) have reshaped Mexico’s investment landscape. The new framework guarantees the state at least 54% of the electricity injected into the grid and gives a central role to mixed-investment projects involving the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) and private companies.

GlobalData has identified a pipeline of power generation projects exceeding 45 GW, dominated by solar PV. However, it warned that transmission and distribution losses, estimated at around 11.5%, and congestion on transmission lines connecting northern Mexico with demand centers in central Mexico and the Bajío region could slow the connection of new projects to the grid.

“Mexico is not lacking in projects or resources. The pace of the transition will depend on whether the mixed-investment model can attract international developers – following years of regulatory uncertainty – and on whether the CFE can expand transmission infrastructure quickly enough,” said Saibasan.

articles.title: China’s TOPCon solar module export prices slip as makers clear low-efficiency stock ahead of new standard
articles.description: In a new weekly update for pv magazine, OPIS, a Dow Jones company, provides a quick look at the main price trends in the global PV industry.
paragraphs: Free-On-Board (FOB) China mainstream module prices edged lower this week, weighed down by continued price weakness in lower-efficiency modules, as manufacturers clear inventories ahead of a stricter module efficiency standard taking effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Industry sources noted that manufacturers have stepped up inventory clearance efforts in the fourth quarter, anticipating weaker domestic offtake for lower-efficiency modules once the new standard comes into effect. Under the standard, the minimum efficiency for TOPCon modules sold in China will be 23.2%, corresponding to a power output of 630 W.

Major producers’ inventories of lower-efficiency modules are already running low, one leading manufacturer said, as most have shifted production lines toward higher-efficiency products and average module power ratings among major TOPCon producers have reached around 640 W. Most of the remaining lower-efficiency stock sits with smaller or tier-2 players, who are undercutting prices aggressively, the manufacturer said.

A top-tier integrated module manufacturer said aggressive discounting in the lower-efficiency segment has also placed downward pressure on mainstream module prices, as procurement teams increasingly use lower-priced offers as leverage in price negotiations. The manufacturer added that while policies aimed at curbing module oversupply and regulating prices could support the market over the longer term, intense price competition among manufacturers is likely to persist in the near term.
Meanwhile, a divergence between domestic and export module prices has become increasingly evident since the start of Q4 2026.

Domestic mainstream TOPCon module prices have softened amid weakening demand, while export prices have remained comparatively resilient, with market sources noting that manufacturers’ quotations for overseas markets have largely resisted the downward trend in domestic prices.

According to OPIS data, EXW China TOPCon module prices fell by more than 1.8% since the beginning of October, while FOB China TOPCon mainstream modules remained broadly unchanged, before edging down by 0.93% this week.

Senate clears permitting reform after a bitter split among greens
articles.description: The bill could speed up major energy projects like solar farms, transmission lines, and gas pipelines.
paragraphs: The Senate on Thursday, in a 62-33 vote, passed a bipartisan permitting reform bill that aims to speed up the construction of major energy infrastructure like clean energy, transmission lines, and gas pipelines.

Passage of the Bipartisan Affordability and American Jobs Act was far from guaranteed. It took years of negotiations and caused a split within the climate movement, exposing fractures among green groups. Both clean and fossil fuel energy developers, among other business groups, were immediately on board. But four key senators also had to make changes in recent weeks to address concerns from Tribes, investor-owned utilities, and environmentalists in order to win more votes.

Those changes were enough to sway the utility industry’s lobbying group, The Edison Electric Institute, and the climate advocacy group Evergreen Action. But nearly every Democratic member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee ultimately voted against it on Thursday, excluding Rhode Island Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a lead negotiator of the deal. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) also voted no, in part over provisions narrowing Tribes’ consultation rights with the federal government over cultural and sacred sites.

The bill now heads the House, where a coalition of more than 100 moderate Democrats are warming to it. Some other members, including Reps. Jared Huffman (Calif.) and Rashida Tlaib (Mich.), are opposed and argue the party should hold out until next year when it controls Congress.

Supporters of BAAJA said this is their best shot at passing permitting reform, given President Donald Trump still has two years left in office and would likely veto a version pushed by Democrats. They also argue that enacting permitting reform is a way to deliver results as soon as possible for U.S. voters demanding that politicians make their lives more affordable and make data centers pay for their energy costs.

“We cannot keep holding out on permitting reform year after year, in the hopes that maybe, just maybe, we’re going to do it a little bit better next time,” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said during floor debate. “This is our best option, not only for now, but likely for years to come.”

There’s widespread agreement that it takes far too long to build energy projects in the U.S. The skyrocketing power demands of data centers, reshored manufacturing, and greater electrification of transportation and other industries has added new urgency to permitting reform. Utilities also need to continue upgrading the existing grid so it’s more resilient to extreme weather as global temperatures rise, primarily from burning fossil fuels.

BAAJA would set faster timelines for federal agencies to review and approve environmental permits for a long list of energy projects, as well as shorten the window parties have to sue from years to 150 days. The bill would also make it harder for courts to block projects under the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act, and Endangered Species Act. For example, construction could continue even if a court rules that a federal environmental review was deficient. Another section narrows the authority that states and Tribes have to deny projects over water pollution.

articles.title: How clean energy developers can shield against stranded AI power
articles.description: Cypress Creek CEO Kevin Smith on the tricky commercial terms of islanded power for data centers.
paragraphs: In the last two years, expectations that any meaningful portion of new data centers will operate entirely islanded from the grid have been significantly tempered. But data center developers are still embracing off-grid power solutions to help get online more quickly.
While gas will be the dominant source of power, according to analysis from Latitude Intelligence, clean energy developers see an opportunity, too.

Building islanded power projects introduces new risks. But Kevin Smith, CEO of Cypress Creek Energy, a developer that builds solar and storage, said that company would be willing to do off-grid deals, providing certain commercial terms are met.

The company’s strong preference is to build projects that then sell power directly to the grid, Smith explained. That’s because doing an off-grid project “is like 3X the complexity of doing a grid-connected project, especially when you look at the reliability requirements that the hyperscalers are looking for in their data center.”

But there are a few contract terms that could shift the risks enough to make an off-grid project amenable to the company, Smith added. They include a guarantee that protects Cypress Creek’s investment if the data center doesn’t end up needing the power or pulls back early, and limits on the penalties Cypress Creek would face for failing to deliver the promised reliability. Such protections ensure the company isn’t on the hook for costs if a hyperscaler leaves.

Hyperscalers generally require “five nines” of reliability — nearly 100% uptime — and substantial pre-determined damages if the supplier falls short, Smith explained. “That’s technically very difficult to do.”
He added that power facilities have a 30- to 40-year useful life. But it’s less clear how quickly data centers become outdated, which is an added risk for off-grid power projects.

“Does that data center become outdated in five years? And now you’ve got a 40-year power plant attached to a five- to seven-year data center,” he said. “If you’re grid connected and you have a problem with your power contract, you can always find another buyer for that power.”

For now, Cypress Creek’s largest data center-connected project follows Smith’s preferred grid-tied model. The Steel River Energy Center in Mississippi County, Arkansas will send its power to the grid via Entergy Arkansas, rather than directly to Google’s data centers in the region. Google is an anchor investor and offtaker for its first two phases, which are expected to add 1.6 GWdc of solar generation and 1.9 GWh of battery storage to the regional grid. The full three-phase project is expected to reach 2.5 GW of solar and 2.9 GWh of storage when fully operational in 2029.

It’s not only off-grid solutions spurring concerns about stranded infrastructure. Front-of-meter projects are, too, which is already reshaping utility service agreements. A Latitude Intelligence analysis earlier this year found that tariffs increasingly include minimum bills, long-term commitments, and collateral requirements. Fifteen of 25 tariffs examined in the analysis included numerical billing floors, averaging around 80% of contracted demand.

articles.title: How would Becerra’s solar Power Hour actually work?
articles.description: The governor-elect wants to tap California’s solar bounty to reduce midday bills. Utility rate design experts are figuring out the details.
paragraphs: During his campaign, Becerra said that if elected, he would institute a policy offering up to two hours of free electricity in the middle of each day, a move that his administration says could cut utility bills by about $ 1, 000 a year. The proposal has won accolades from clean energy luminaries like former Michigan Gov. and Biden administration Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, former California Public Utilities Commissioner Cliff Rechtschaffen, and UC Santa Barbara professor and author Leah Stokes, who explained why it’s so exciting at last week’s Canary Live Bay Area event.

Free midday rates could encourage people to use more electricity at times when solar power is abundant, so much so that it’s being increasingly curtailed, especially during mild spring and autumn days, often driving wholesale power prices into negative territory. That makes free power ​ “ actually possible in California,” said Claudine Custodio, regulatory director for the West at nonprofit Vote Solar.
But the devil is in the details, so utility rate design experts have been busy figuring out how it could actually work.

The first step is to ​ “ make it as simple and easy to understand as possible,” said Michael Colvin, director of regulatory and legislative affairs at the Environmental Defense Fund. While at the California Public Utilities Commission ( CPUC ), he helped design the time-of-use rates now used by the state’s big three investor-owned utilities, which charge more for power during the evening, when solar production fades and the state’s grid faces its greatest stress.
That rate switch has been complicated enough for customers, Colvin said. Matching rates to seasonal shifts in those peak power costs ​ “ would be a messaging nightmare.”
The same lesson should apply to Power Hour. Even if wholesale power is cheaper in the spring and fall than it is in the winter or summer, the hours of free electricity should stay the same, he said.

That brings up another issue: Just because there’s excess solar power on California’s grid doesn’t make it free to deliver to households. Wholesale power costs make up only about one-third of the typical rates charged by California’s big utilities. The majority of monthly bills goes toward covering fixed costs — mainly those associated with building and maintaining power grids.

Cutting customers’ bills to zero cents per kilowatt-hour for two hours a day will force utilities to increase rates at other times or find alternative ways to make up for income they’d lose during that period. And Becerra has made clear that his plan can’t push total costs higher.

That could be why Becerra has proposed starting by offering free electricity during certain hours only to families eligible for CARE (California Alternate Rates for Energy) and FERA (Family Electric Rate Assistance). Every utility regulated by the CPUC must provide these discount programs for income-qualified households, and the money to pay for those discounts is collected from charges on all other customers’ bills.

The ID. Buzz brings the classic Type 2 microbus into the electric era with a retro-new style, modern tech, and a flexible, spacious cabin.
Building on its reputation as a symbol of freedom and adventure, Volkswagen is adding a new member to the electric people mover lineup.

The new ID. Buzz Beach “brings adventure into the electric age,” Volkswagen said after introducing the new variant on Thursday. Designed for camping, longer road trips, and overnight stays, the electric van will be available in 5-, 6-, and 7-seat configurations.

It also includes blackout curtains throughout the cabin and ventilation grilles on the front side windows.

The ID. Buzz Beach offers vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities. A 230V power socket adaptor comes standard, letting you power an e-bike, charge a smartphone, run camping equipment, or power other external electronic devices. A camping connector is available as an added option.

SolarEdge debuts dual-module power optimizer
articles.description: Duo cuts the number of optimizers needed in half, works with dual-tilt racking and with Arc Fault Detection, every optimizer becomes an arc sensor.
paragraphs: SolarEdge unveiled its new U.S.-made Duo power optimizer for commercial and industrial (C&I) solar projects this week at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas.

Power optimizers are DC-to-DC converters installed on the underside of solar modules to maximize power output. Unlike conventional optimizers, which typically connect to a single module, the SolarEdge Duo connects to two modules, with an independent maximum power point tracker (MPPT) for each.

According to the company’s datasheet, each input supports up to 650 W, with an MPPT operating voltage range of 12.5 V to 57 V and a maximum continuous input current of 20 A. The optimizer has a maximum output voltage of 80 V, a maximum output current of 20 A and a weighted efficiency of 98.8%.

SolarEdge said the dual-module design reduces the number of optimizers required by 50% compared with its C651U model. Each optimizer features a short pair of wires for the nearest module and a pre-extended pair for the adjacent module, reducing cable slack and eliminating the need for field-installed jumpers. The Duo also supports dual-tilt racking configurations, allowing it to connect modules facing different directions.

The device measures 129 mm x 159 mm x 59 mm and weighs 1.2 kg, including cables. It has an IP68/NEMA 6P protection rating and an operating temperature range of -40 C to 85 C, with power derating above 65 C. The optimizer supports a maximum system voltage of 1,000 V and is compatible with specified SolarEdge commercial three-phase inverters.

The Duo features SolarEdge’s optimizer-level arc fault detection technology, which uses each optimizer as an arc sensor as part of the company’s arc fault circuit interruption (AFCI) system. According to SolarEdge, this enables arc faults to be detected closer to their source rather than solely at the inverter. If one optimizer fails to detect an arc, a neighboring optimizer can detect it, the company said. The system reportedly provides protection for strings with a total cable length of up to 1,000 meters between the inverter and optimizers.
SolarEdge reports that its Sense Connect technology also monitors temperature at every input and output connector to identify developing faults.
The Duo comes with a 25-year warranty. Manufactured in Florida, it is designed to meet U.S. Domestic Content and Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements.

The Duo power optimizer is available to order now in the U.S. through SolarEdge sales channels and distribution partners, with shipments expected to begin in January 2027. SolarEdge is showing the Duo this week at RE+ in booth N1516.

articles.title: Aptera (SEV) completes its first customer solar EV
articles.description: Aptera completed its first solar EV for a customer, but it goes to its top investor overseas while the startup still needs $25M to start production.
paragraphs: Aptera (SEV) has finished building its first solar electric vehicle for a paying customer. It’s going to Martin Hartono, the startup’s No. 1 “Accelerator” investor, and it’s being exported out of the US.

Aptera announced today from its Carlsbad, California headquarters that it completed what it calls its first production solar electric vehicle. The car is finished in “Noir,” a matte black exterior, and was built for Accelerator #1.
Accelerators are investors from Aptera’s community funding program, where delivery priority goes to whoever invests the most. So the first customer car went to the biggest check.

Hartono is the CEO of GDP Venture, the Jakarta-based venture arm of Indonesia’s Djarum Group. Aptera didn’t say which country the car is going to, what he paid for it, or when it will actually be handed over.

In the release, Hartono said Aptera is a fit for people who want to “minimize their energy consumption without compromising the ability to travel long distances.” Co-CEO Chris Anthony called it “the moment our team has worked toward for years” and said the company is working to finish more vehicles for early customers as soon as possible.

The solar side of the pitch holds up better. In August, TÜV Rheinland measured 4.23 to 4.75 kWh per day going into the battery from the car’s integrated panels in Carlsbad, which works out to roughly 40 miles of daily driving. But that conversion relies on Aptera’s 100 Wh/mile efficiency target, and today’s release itself notes that figure isn’t yet confirmed for production vehicles.

The release’s risk factors are also worth reading. They list export, import, certification and registration requirements, state dealer licensing, single-source suppliers, and whether reservations will convert into binding orders. Shipping car No. 1 to an investor overseas sidesteps most of those for now.

Credit where it’s due. Aptera has a finished car built to a customer’s spec, which is more than Lightyear or Sono Motors ever got to before they ran out of money. We’ve followed this company since it came back in 2019, and plenty of people (us included, at times) didn’t think we’d see this day.

But I have to be honest, this looks more symbolic than like the start of a production ramp. This is a single vehicle, built before Aptera has raised the money it says it needs for series production, and it went to the person who put the most money into the company. That’s a thank-you and a good press release ahead of what will likely be another raise. It doesn’t tell us much about Aptera’s ability to build cars at a cost that works.

We want this to work. Ultra-efficient cars are the only way vehicle-integrated solar makes sense, and Aptera is the last serious attempt standing. So can it fund those 40 cars before the cash runs out?

articles.title: MicroQuanta, Zhejiang University achieve world-record efficiency of 23.9% for 19.48 cm² perovskite solar module
articles.description: The result was certified by the National PV Industry Measurement and Testing Center (NPVM) of China’s Fujian Metrology Institute.
paragraphs: A research team led by scientists from Chinese perovskite solar cell manufacturer MicroQuanta Semiconductor has achieved a certified steady-state efficiency of 23.9% for a 19.48 cm² perovskite mini-module, setting a new world record.

The researchers said the result was enabled by cooling the wet perovskite precursor film before vacuum treatment to slow crystallization and reduce the fill factor losses associated with scaling up from cells to modules.

“What makes our result special is that the world record is achieved at the module level, rather than in a small laboratory cell,” corresponding author Dongchen Lan told pv magazine. “Solar cells often lose efficiency when scaled up into modules.”
The result was certified by the National PV Industry Measurement and Testing Center (NPVM) of China’s Fujian Metrology Institute.

Lan said the team identified a major cause of these losses and demonstrated a way to mitigate them while helping modules maintain their performance over time. “This addresses a key challenge in bringing next-generation solar technologies closer to practical use,” he said.

The researchers first compared laboratory-scale perovskite solar cells with mini-modules fabricated under matched processing conditions in previous studies. They used Shapley value analysis, which averages the contribution of each parameter across all possible orders of substitution, to quantify the contributions of open-circuit voltage, short-circuit current density, and fill factor to the measured efficiency loss.
After accounting for current losses in inactive areas created by laser scribing, they found that fill factor was the largest contributor to the efficiency drop from cells to modules.

To reduce that loss, the team spin-coated a perovskite precursor onto indium tin oxide (ITO)-coated glass carrying two hole-transport layers (HTLs). Immediately after coating, they cooled the wet film for 15 seconds to 0-10 C, transferred it to a vacuum chamber within about five seconds, and vacuum-flashed it for two minutes before annealing it at 110 C for 30 minutes. They then applied a surface passivation layer and deposited the electron-transport layers (ETLs) and silver (Ag) electrode. Measurements during film formation showed that cooling slowed the conversion of an intermediate phase into perovskite, yielding films with larger, more uniform grains.

The researchers used slot-die coating to fabricate a 19.48 cm² perovskite mini-module consisting of eight subcells connected in series through laser scribing. The device was built on a glass substrate coated with indium tin oxide (ITO), nickel oxide (NiOₓ), and a self-assembled monolayer known as 3PATAT-C3. It featured a formamidinium-cesium lead iodide (FA₀.₉₅Cs₀.₀₅PbI₃) absorber with an ethylenediammonium diiodide (EDAI₂) surface passivation layer, a fullerene (C₆₀) electron transport layer, a bathocuproine (BCP) buffer layer, and a silver (Ag) electrode.

According to the team’s measurements, the mini-module achieved a certified steady-state efficiency of 23.9% and a fill factor of 83.3%, which the authors reported as the highest for a perovskite module. It also had a geometric fill factor of 97%, meaning 97% of its aperture area was photoactive. In separate aging tests under continuous one-sun illumination at open-circuit, the efficiency loss attributable to declining fill factor was less than one-third as large in modules made with the cooling step as in control modules.

articles.description: The German manufacturer's new glass-glass solar panel features back-contact cells, a power conversion efficiency of 23.8% and a bifaciality factor of approximately 70%. It comes with a 30-year product warranty and an 88.85% power output guarantee after 30 years.
paragraphs: German solar module manufacturer Solyco has introduced a new full-black, glass-glass solar module for residential applications.

The Solyco Design R-BG 108nBC.6 Protect panel features a stainless steel cover for its connection cables, designed to protect them against mechanical damage, animal bites and ultraviolet (UV) radiation.

The module features 108 monocrystalline half-cut cells based on back-contact (BC) technology, delivering a power output of 485 W and a conversion efficiency of 23.8%. Under standard test conditions (STC), it has a maximum power voltage of 33.94 V and a maximum power current of 14.30 A. Its open-circuit voltage is 40.89 V, while its short-circuit current is 15.03 A.

The back-contact cell design places electrical connections on the rear of the cells, reducing front-side shading and providing a full-black appearance. The module has a bifaciality factor of around 70%. It features three separate junction boxes, each equipped with a bypass diode, with an IP68 protection rating. The 4 mm² solar cables are 1.2 m long and fitted with Stäubli MC4-Evo 2 connectors.
The module measures 1,800 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm and weighs 24.8 kg. It features 2 mm tempered solar glass on both sides and a black-anodized aluminum frame.
The operating temperature ranges from -40 C to 85 C, with a nominal module operating temperature (NMOT) of 42 C. The temperature coefficient is -0.26%/C.

The module supports a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V and a maximum reverse current of 30 A. It can withstand front-side loads of up to 5,400 Pa and rear-side loads of up to 2,400 Pa. The manufacturer also claims resistance to hailstones measuring up to 30 mm in diameter at impact speeds of 23.9 m/s.
Solyco offers a product warranty of up to 30 years and guarantees 88.85% of the module’s initial power output after 30 years.
According to the manufacturer, the R-BG 108nBC.6 Protect is its first commercially available module featuring integrated protection against animal bites for its connection cables.

Berlin-based Solyco Solar has expanded its portfolio of high-efficiency PV modules and specialized solar technologies in recent years. In July 2026, the company introduced a 500 W full-black back-contact module with an efficiency of 24.5%, following the launch of a 480 W back-contact panel in August 2025. The company has also developed a low-temperature solar cell interconnection technology designed to reduce material costs and vertical PV systems for green rooftops.

Jackery and Every Electric launch 4 MWh plug-in battery VPP for New York renters
articles.description: Jackery has partnered with Brooklyn-based aggregator Every Electric to shift air conditioning load peaks without permitting limitations.
paragraphs: Portable power station manufacturer Jackery and consumer energy aggregator Every Electric have partnered to roll out what they call North America’s first plug-in battery aimed at renters and apartment residents.
By aggregating behind-the-meter storage, the setup uses standard wall outlets rather than hardwired residential systems that require electricians.

The tie-up is part of an Every Electric program that has operated across Consolidated Edison’s New York City service territory since September. Roughly 2,000 portable power stations, mostly Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, are currently distributed across more than 1,000 households, providing 4 MWh of flexible storage capacity. According to the companies, nearly 50 MWh of energy has cycled through the units to date.
The companies are calling it the “continent’s first plug-and-play virtual power plant (VPP) distribution network based on self-contained, expandable portable power stations”.

Onboarding requires residents to register online, link their utility account, and plug a window or portable air conditioner into the drop-shipped battery’s passthrough outlet. Once connected to Wi-Fi via Jackery’s app, Every Electric’s cloud software automates charging during off-peak hours and discharges the battery to run the air conditioner during peak grid demand, while keeping backup capacity available for outages.
The setup is similar to how plug-in storage has worked in Europe’s balcony solar market, and requires no electrician labor, municipal permits, or other agreements.
Every Electric offers options, both tied to a portable battery and an air conditioning unit.

A third option appears to be accepting a BYO battery as well, and Every Electric has details of operating with other brands outside of Jackery, with photos showing EcoFlow and Bluetti portable power stations.

“Traditional solar and storage require a roof, a garage or a permanent professional installation, which leaves renters and multifamily residents out,” said Andrew Wang, co-founder and CEO of Every Electric. “With Every Electric, adding grid services capabilities lets any household with a wall outlet earn on their bills while supporting the broader electrical infrastructure.”

Both companies are demonstrating the platform at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas from November 17 to 19, where Jackery is also exhibiting its modular Explorer 5000 Plus system with smart transfer switch support.

articles.title: Tesla seeks Texas tax break for $3.1 billion polysilicon plant
articles.description: Tesla says it will build a polysilicon plant in Texas only if the state cuts its property tax bill, as it seeks to produce solar’s most China-dominated material at home.
paragraphs: The application, filed with the Tuloso-Midway Independent School District under the state’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) program, has been published by the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts.

Tesla describes the plant as “under consideration for development” and as the “upstream component of Tesla’s vertically integrated domestic solar manufacturing platform.” It says that “in the absence of the agreement the applicant would not make the proposed investment in this state” and that it is assessing locations in other jurisdictions.

The plant would produce ultra-high-purity polysilicon for single-crystal silicon ingots and N-type, high-efficiency solar cells. Its equipment list includes a hydrochlorination and trichlorosilane synthesis unit, chlorosilane distillation and purification trains, silicon tetrachloride recycling loops and Siemens chemical vapor deposition reactors. The filing does not state the plant’s production capacity.
Tesla said in the filing that more than 90% of the world’s solar-grade polysilicon is produced in China.

Under the schedule in the EY analysis, the project’s taxable value for school-district maintenance and operations taxes would be cut to zero from 2028 to 2030 and halved from 2031 through 2040. The Comptroller must review the application, and both the Office of the Governor and the school district’s board must approve an agreement before it takes effect.

The US government’s Section 232 tariffs and minimum import prices on polysilicon, which also impose a 15% duty on imported ingots, wafers, cells and modules, take effect on Dec. 4. The minimum import prices are designed to force foreign suppliers to match US production costs, raising the value of domestic feedstock in a market where US polysilicon production remains limited. Solar manufacturer Toyo secured US polysilicon supply to navigate trade barriers in January.

Tesla has been advancing a plan to build 100 GW of US PV manufacturing capacity by 2028, a target that has drawn scrutiny over whether Elon Musk’s solar ambitions are achievable. The company has taken a similar approach in storage, where it said in 2025 that its 10 GWh lithium iron phosphate cell factory in Nevada was nearing completion as it reduced reliance on imported cells.

LONGi actively promotes the “energy + rural revitalization” development model in many developing regions. For example, since 2024, Shaanxi Province has been rolling out the “PV+” rural revitalization demonstration project, under which the government provides overall coordination; village collectives establish village-owned new energy companies as the investment and loan entities; and farming households only provide rooftop space and bear no investment or loan risk. For remote regions with inadequate grid infrastructure, LONGi deploys off-grid and microgrid solar-storage systems, using clean energy to light up remote villages, ensure electricity for local healthcare, education, and people’s basic daily needs, and help address energy accessibility challenges in certain areas.

SCP studies estimate that the canals could accommodate more than 50 MW of PV capacity, generating approximately 70 GWh of electricity annually.

paragraphs: Indonesia’s cumulative installed solar capacity reached 1.59 GW as of the first quarter of 2026 (Q1 2026), according to the latest report from the Institute for Essential Services Reform (IESR), a Jakarta-based think tank.
IESR’s Indonesia Solar Energy Outlook 2027 says the figure is equivalent to around 1.5% of Indonesia’s power generation capacity and 0.3% of electricity production.

Rooftop PV currently accounts for the largest share of installed capacity, standing at 0.9 GW as of Q1 2026. Utility-scale solar accounted for 0.33 GW, captive solar for 0.3 GW and installations in remote areas for around 0.06 GW.

With the country passing the 1 GW solar milestone in 2025, IESR says the current growth rate is “far behind the government’s ambition to make solar power one of the backbones of the national energy system”, as set out in the country’s 100 GW solar power program which President Prabowo Subianto has set a target of achieving by 2029.
The program officially launched in August with a first phase of 14 projects totalling around 5.2 GW, but only 526 MW of this capacity currently have targeted completion dates, IESR’s report reveals.
The think tank adds that deployments are currently held back by regulatory gaps, procurement uncertainty and limited grid access.

In a statement sent to pv magazine, IESR CEO Fabby Tumiwa said the 100 GW ambition needs to be reflected in updates to Indonesia’s 2025-2034 electricity supply business plan (RUPTL), with greater emphasis on utility-scale PV and battery energy storage systems (BESS), diesel replacement with solar-plus-storage and rooftop PV deployment.
IESR’s modelling suggests Indonesia could reach 96.7 GW of solar capacity by 2029 if development proceeds through multiple channels simultaneously.

The report says around 8 GW is already planned through RUPTL and Mentari GigaOne procurements, while a further 56 GW could come through procurements by Indonesia’s state-owned electric utility PLN. It suggests the remaining 33 GW could be developed through rooftop PV, diesel replacement, rural electrification, captive solar and other distributed applications.
IESR says five enablers that must move together – demand, rooftop access, procurement, grid and supply chain – will determine whether the 100 GW scales.

Efficient heating is not enough: Why the timing of electricity use matters for heat pumps
articles.description: Operating a heat pump as cost-effectively as possible involves more than just monitoring electricity prices. In many cases, shifting electricity consumption to different times is neither feasible nor practical. Matthias Martensen, CEO and co-founder of Ostrom, explains the factors that determine how flexibly heat pumps can use electricity.
paragraphs: When discussing the cost-effectiveness of heat pumps, the focus is usually on the seasonal performance factor (SPF), flow temperature and building insulation. While these factors remain crucial, the debate around dynamic electricity tariffs is too narrow if it focuses solely on how long a heat pump can be switched off. What matters is the overall flexibility of a household’s electricity consumption.

On very cold winter days, well-designed heat pumps often need to run almost continuously, leaving little scope for shifting heat production. At milder temperatures, however, there is some flexibility: Buildings and hot water storage tanks can retain heat for several hours. For example, a home can be preheated overnight for the morning or during the day for the evening. Similarly, hot water production can be scheduled for periods when electricity prices are lower. How long this flexibility lasts depends on the building’s insulation, heating system and storage capacity, although it is generally insufficient to bridge entire days.

Even when a heat pump runs continuously, the electricity it consumes does not necessarily have to be drawn from the grid at the same time. A suitable battery storage system can charge from the grid when electricity prices are low and supply power later. In this case, it is not heat production that is shifted, but the timing of electricity drawn from the grid. This distinction is particularly relevant for households with photovoltaic systems and existing battery storage.

In summer, PV systems cover a larger share of household electricity demand with self-generated solar power. In winter, heating demand increases while solar power generation declines, making households more dependent on grid electricity. An existing battery storage system, provided it supports grid charging and can be controlled in response to electricity prices, can therefore do more than store solar power. It can also take advantage of periods of low wholesale electricity prices.

For households that already have battery storage, the economics are different. The key question is whether the potential savings from price differences outweigh additional storage losses, battery degradation and any costs associated with technical modifications. Even then, profitable operation is far from guaranteed. Average hourly prices also do not reflect the price differences that can actually be exploited on individual days. While the figures illustrate the importance of when electricity is drawn from the grid, they do not demonstrate actual savings.

Other flexible loads also play a role. Households charging electric vehicles, particularly in winter, often cannot rely solely on electricity generated by their own PV systems. Coordinated energy management can help shift charging to periods when grid electricity is cheaper. Even when solar generation is low, strong wind power output can drive down wholesale electricity prices.

For heat pumps, electricity prices are not the only factor affecting operating costs. With air-to-water heat pumps, outdoor temperatures also matter. If temperatures are higher around midday than in the early morning, the system can operate more efficiently. An intelligent control system should therefore consider electricity prices, outdoor temperatures and actual heating demand simultaneously. Producing additional heat simply because electricity is cheap makes little sense if that heat is ultimately wasted.
articles.lede: Operating a heat pump as cost-effectively as possible involves more than just monitoring electricity prices. In many cases, shifting electricity consumption to different times is neither feasible nor practical.

articles.title: Wisconsin’s new Dem trifecta could be a boon for clean energy
articles.description: The state lags behind its neighbors in transitioning to renewables. Now policymakers have the chance to overcome logjams on community solar and more.
paragraphs: The Democratic sweep in this year’s midterm elections has opened up new opportunities for advancing the clean energy transition in states across the country. That’s particularly true in Wisconsin, where Democrats will have a trifecta for the first time in 16 years, and which has lagged behind its Midwestern neighbors on renewables.

Indeed, Gov.-elect David Crowley (D) and legislative leaders have pledged to promote clean energy as a way to address affordability and meet demand from planned data centers. Advocates say they have already been talking with legislators and drafting proposals that they hope will advance once new lawmakers take office on Jan. 4.

“ It’s very exciting to see these changes,” said Beata Wierzba, government affairs director at RENEW Wisconsin, a nonprofit advocacy group that works to advance clean energy policies. ​ “ The Democratic leadership has a very ambitious agenda, which includes clean energy and renewables. We know we’re on their plate.”

Last spring, Democratic state lawmakers introduced a bill mandating that Wisconsin electricity generation be 100 % emissions-free by 2050. The bill did not advance, but clean energy advocates are hoping a similar initiative will be a top priority for the new Democratic legislature. The only such mandate on the books right now is woefully outdated, calling for 10 % renewable energy by 2015. The state has long surpassed that, with a fifth of the electricity delivered to customers currently coming from renewables.

Shifting to net-zero emissions by 2050 — including 100 % clean energy — would create over 68, 000 jobs and avoid at least $ 2 billion in healthcare costs, according to a report by RENEW, the nonprofit Clean Wisconsin, and other groups.

Abby Novinska-Lois, executive director of the nonprofit public health advocacy group Healthy Climate Wisconsin, noted that ​ “ Wisconsin is really behind” states like Illinois — which mandates fossil-fuel-free electricity generation by 2045 — when it comes to emissions that harm the climate and public health.

“ We think all Wisconsinites deserve the freedom to have cleaner air and cleaner water and the [lower] bills that come with clean energy,” she said. ​ “ We are hearing interest from policymakers that they want to accelerate affordable energy for all Wisconsinites. We know clean energy is the most affordable.”

Right now in Wisconsin, only utilities can build solar arrays that provide energy to customers. Twenty-four states plus Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico, allow companies other than utilities to build community solar, including Wisconsin’s neighbor Illinois, which provides robust incentives.
“ Now with the Democratic majority, we might be able to work something out where both sides will see it’s good for the workers and good for the people,” Wierzba said.

For almost a decade, Wisconsin has been a battleground over third-party-owned distributed solar. Under such arrangements, a solar developer owns the array that provides power to a home, business, organization, or government agency. The model eliminates up-front costs for the customer and helps nonprofits and government entities tap tax incentives that might not otherwise be available since they don’t pay taxes. But the state’s largest utility, We Energies, has long argued that this lets solar developers illegally act as utilities. Solar advocates and developers want a law to clarify that third-party-owned solar is legal so that projects can move forward.
articles.lede: The state lags behind its neighbors in transitioning to renewables. Now policymakers have the chance to overcome logjams on community solar and more.

articles.title: Massachusetts pilot program offers free batteries and extra cash
articles.description: In Fall River, low-income families can receive a free home battery and a yearly stipend as part of a utility program to reduce grid strain and electricity…
paragraphs: A Massachusetts utility has announced plans to use home batteries to help 125 low-income families save money and keep the lights on during power outages — all at no cost to them. If successful, the pilot program could serve as a model for similar initiatives throughout the state, as utilities pursue a mandate to create a more affordable, robust, and equitable electric system.

National Grid this month launched BatteryBackup+, a partnership with residential power-storage company Haven Energy that will bring the no-cost batteries to homes in Fall River, a working-class former mill city where the median household income hovers just above half the statewide average.

Participants will receive a battery capable of providing at least four hours of backup power, as well as $ 150 annually for five years. To qualify, residents must already be signed up for National Grid’s low-income discount rate, or meet the equivalent income limits — about $ 103, 000 per year for a four-person household, for example.

Haven will handle installation and maintenance of the systems, and manage the batteries’ enrollment and deployment in programs that share their power with the grid to alleviate strain at times of high demand. After 10 years, participants will be able to work with Haven to take over ownership and management of the batteries or remove them. The utility’s overall goal is to develop and refine a strategy for making the grid more efficient and resilient while giving a financial boost to families who are the most vulnerable to soaring energy prices.
“ We’re really excited about what we get to learn from this,” said Joshua Tom, National Grid’s director of energy transition solutions.

The idea of aggregating residential batteries to create benefits for the grid is not new. When batteries work in concert to send power into the system, it can reduce the need for energy from pricier, dirtier plants. In the long term, such arrangements can also help avoid expensive grid upgrades that would be paid for by customers.

States are increasingly leaning into the concept. Vermont’s Green Mount Power harnesses this potential with a network of 10, 000 residential batteries. Massachusetts’ ConnectedSolutions model, launched as a pilot in 2016, has been adopted or adapted by nearby states including Connecticut and Rhode Island. New Jersey just launched its own program paying residents to share their battery capacity with the grid.

Haven’s business model takes advantage of this trend. As in the Fall River pilot, the company handles the installation and management of residential batteries. Haven then earns money from enrolling the equipment in state programs, using some of the revenue to make the investment more affordable for customers.

Haven currently operates in seven states — including elsewhere in Massachusetts — with eight more coming soon. In most places, customers pay a monthly fee for their batteries and the company’s services, starting at $ 29.

Fall River is not Haven’s first foray into a no-cost model. Last year, the company launched a program in California providing free batteries to low-income households. So far, the program has contracted with about 2, 500 homes and completed installations in about 60 % of them.
articles.lede: A Massachusetts utility has announced plans to use home batteries to help 125 low-income families save money and keep the lights on during power outages — all at no cost to them.

articles.title: How solar and storage are powering a new era of American manufacturing
articles.description: The Steel River Energy Center in Arkansas will help supply electricity to U. S. Steel’s Big River Steel mill, offering a model for how utility-scale…
paragraphs: In the early 2020 s, U. S. Steel launched a nationwide search to find the best location for a new factory. The company had recently completed its acquisition of the Big River Steel mill in Osceola, Arkansas. The goal of the expansion: Replicate the success of Big River Steel, which supplies the automotive, construction, and renewable-energy industries and can produce over 3 million tons of steel annually.

After an exhaustive search, the company realized there was no reason to look beyond Northeast Arkansas. ​ “ We went to 48 states and narrowed the site selection down to 20, 10, five, and then three,” said Dan Brown, U. S. Steel’s executive vice president of advanced technology steelmaking and CEO of Big River Steel. ​ “ We built another plant one mile from where we’re at.” At close to $ 3. 5 billion, the investment in what is now called Big River Steel 2 was the largest in U. S. Steel’s storied 125 -year history.

A variety of factors go into determining the ideal location of a steel plant, including proximity to large customers, good railroad and river transportation, and a solid local workforce. Arguably most important, however, is access to reliable and affordable electricity, because producing steel requires an enormous amount of power. ​ “ If that isn’t number one, it’s in the top two,” Brown said. ​ “ You have to have a good electricity provider and a good electricity source.”

The reliable, affordable energy source that will help power the growth of one of America’s most iconic manufacturers is solar and energy storage. To that end, the Steel River Energy Center, which broke ground this past July, is a 2. 46 -gigawatt solar and 2. 94 -gigawatt-hour battery storage facility that will be built in three phases and is expected to be fully operational in 2029. Cypress Creek Energy is developing, and will own and operate, what will be the largest solar project with energy storage in America.

The Steel River Energy Center is notable for a host of reasons. The grid-connected project represents $ 4. 5 billion in private investment and is expected to create 1, 400 construction jobs in its first two phases and generate $ 300 million in local tax revenue over its lifetime. Google also signed a power purchase agreement ( PPA) with Cypress Creek Energy to secure the energy produced by the first two phases of the project. The Steel River Energy Center is the largest solar and storage project Google has sourced energy from worldwide.

Whether it’s the project’s size, offtake agreement, job creation, or tax revenue, much about the Steel River Energy Center attracts superlatives. But less obvious, and more meaningful for U.S. communities far beyond Mississippi County, Arkansas is the example it provides of solar and storage’s ability to power even the most energy-intensive industries and the many benefits of a robust domestic supply chain.

“ Ten years ago, solar was still pretty niche, and battery storage was hardly on the radar,” said Kevin Smith, CEO of Cypress Creek Energy. ​ “ Steel River is proof that solar and storage have crossed a threshold. This is not niche energy dependent on incentives. This is the foundation of American industrial competitiveness, because we can beat alternatives on price and speed, both of which are critical to businesses that depend on affordable and reliable energy.”
