Building our piece of the electric stack
articles.description: A conversation with Sam D’Amico of Impulse.
paragraphs: Collectively, the electric stack (batteries, motors, chips, power electronics) has gotten about 99% cheaper since 1990. It is quietly remaking every machine that turns electricity into motion, heat, or work. Problem is, China makes most of it. Sam D’Amico, co-author of “The Electric Slide” and founder of Impulse Labs, is betting the US can still claim a piece of that stack. He’s starting with a battery-powered induction cooktop. We talk about why domestic manufacturing matters, what America would actually have to build to compete, and how Silicon Valley’s founder world really thinks about climate change, geoengineering included.

Energy analysis and journalism have traditionally focused on the supply side, but in recent years there’s been a welcome turn in the other direction, toward the ongoing revolution in the devices that consume energy. What’s happening, around the world, is an explosion of electrotech. The devices that translate electricity into motion, heat, and work are getting exponentially cheaper, smarter, and more sophisticated.

Electrotech basically comes down to four technologies: batteries, electric motors, chips, and power electronics. Together, that “electric stack” has gotten about 99 percent cheaper since 1990, which is why cars, drones, boats, and stoves keep going electric — and why, eventually, everything is going to go electric.

Currently, China manufactures most of that stack, including roughly three-quarters of the world’s lithium-ion batteries and 90 percent of the magnets that spin the motors. That leaves the US in a weak and perilous position.

One of the co-authors of that essay, Sam D’Amico, is trying to put the theory into practice. His company, Impulse Labs, makes a drool-worthy high-end induction cooktop with a battery built in. That lets it push ten kilowatts per burner while plugging into an ordinary 120V outlet. Impulse is now licensing that core platform to bigger appliance brands, and Sam has his eye on “every mid-sized machine that runs on electricity.”

I thought it would be fun to talk to Sam about why the electric stack matters, why he started with a cooktop, where electrotech might go next, and how much of it America can realistically manufacture at home. Let’s do this.

articles.description: Energy Information Administration - EIA - Official Energy Statistics from the U.S. Government
paragraphs: Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Weekly Petroleum Status Report The U.S. refinery fleet has run at higher-than-normal rates this year, with refinery utilization averaging more than 95% of capacity between May and September, the highest for those months since 1998. Tight global product supplies this year have boosted margins for petroleum products, particularly for diesel, incentivizing the increased run rates.
Since 1991, U.S. refinery utilization has averaged 92% from May to September, compared with 88% across the other seven months.

U.S. refineries tend to run at their highest rates between May and September to boost supply of gasoline for the peak demand season in the summer months. Distillate demand, by contrast, peaks in the fall and winter. Because refineries produce a combination of gasoline and distillates, high summer refinery utilization usually leads to an increase in distillate inventories before seasonal refinery maintenance and the peak distillate demand season.
This year the refinery runs were driven largely by tight global supplies for distillate fuel oil, leading to high international demand for U.S. distillate fuel oil exports.
While refinery utilization was the highest since 1998, total U.S. refinery output was only the highest since 2019 because refining capacity has decreased by 4% since then.
In the first 3 weeks of October, U.S. refinery utilization decreased from its summer highs but remained above the five-year (2021–2025) seasonal average.

Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon falls to its lowest year on record
articles.description: Rates have fallen by three-quarters in Lula’s second term.
paragraphs: This weekend, Brazil’s current president, Lula da Silva, will head to the polls against Flávio Bolsonaro (the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro). It looks like the election will be incredibly tight.
I can’t speak to all of Lula’s record, but there is one area where he has made a clear difference: in reducing deforestation in the Amazon.

The latest annual estimates of deforestation were recently published by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research (INPE). Its PRODES project uses satellite imagery to monitor the clearing of forest in the Legal Amazon. You can find this data here.
It estimates that deforestation over the past year (from August 2025 to July 2026) was around 3,300 square kilometres (km 2 ).
As you can see in the chart below, that’s a substantial fall from last year, and the lowest since records began in 1988.
Deforestation rates in the Brazilian Amazon have gone through various waves in recent decades. Lula has been quite central to some of them.
I’ve plotted the same data — annual deforestation rates — but with the bars labelled by which president was in office at the time.

Lula was president before, during the first decade of the 2000s. During his term, deforestation rates fell by three-quarters from their peak. They remained relatively stable during the next two presidents’ terms, but increased again under Jair Bolsonaro. You can see this in red.
These “peak” rates in the early 2020s were still half the rates of the early 2000s, but much higher than they had been over the previous decade.
Under Lula’s current term, they’ve fallen by roughly three-quarters again. Credit where it’s due, his government can reduce deforestation.

articles.title: Can distributed energy work around American utilities?
articles.description: A conversation with Nick Chaset of Octopus US (and Uplight).
paragraphs: American homes are filling up with batteries, EVs, and smart thermostats that could be coordinated to make the grid cheaper and more reliable — but almost none of them are. To understand why, it helps to watch what happens when the company best in the world at this tries to do it here. In Britain, Octopus Energy has built a giant virtual power plant out of its customers' devices. In the US, it has spent six years running into walls. Now it’s bought Uplight, which runs customer programs for 85 utilities. I talked with Nick Chaset, who runs both, about what's in the way and whether distributed energy can ever scale with US utilities … the way they are.

Distributed energy (rooftop solar, home batteries, EVs, smart thermostats) is accumulating in American homes. In theory, all of it could be coordinated to help the grid, shaving peaks and delaying expensive new infrastructure investments. In practice, very little of it is. Why is that?

One useful way into that question is to look at a company that’s very good at that kind of coordination. In Britain, Octopus Energy is the single largest household electricity supplier; it has turned hundreds of thousands of its customers’ EVs, home batteries, and other devices into a giant virtual power plant. It came to the US in 2020 intending to do something similar. Six years later, it still sells electricity only in Texas.

So it has adapted. It sells flexibility services to utilities, supplies residential capacity to aggregators chasing data-center money, puts batteries in homes for a monthly fee, and, as of September, owns a majority of Uplight, which runs customer-side programs for 85 utilities. Is this all a clever way of routing around America’s dysfunctional market structures? Or is it just an elaborate holding pattern until those structures change?

That’s what I’m going to discuss today with Nick Chaset, CEO of both Octopus Energy US and Uplight. What’s it going to take to scale distributed energy in the US from this kind of random bric-a-brac to an actual, substantial contributor to US electricity? Let’s get into it.

How much could the UK actually raise from higher taxes?
articles.description: The uncomfortable numbers behind Britain’s largest tax levers.
paragraphs: Every time this comes around, there’s intense debate about what financial holes we need to fill, whether we should raise taxes or cut spending, and which taxes we should change or leave untouched. Countless numbers are flying around, and I’ve struggled to find anywhere that puts them into context.
For my own sanity, I wanted to understand how large each tax lever is. Are we talking hundreds of millions, billions, tens of billions?

Running the numbers surprised me. The UK government spends £1.4 trillion a year. Raising the basic rate of income tax by one percentage point would raise £8 billion. The top rate, just £270 million. Estimates for an annual wealth tax (which is far more contested among economists) might raise £10 billion in an optimistic scenario. Not nothing, but less than 1% of current spending.

I’m not arguing that we should raise specific taxes, or even any taxes. That’s a political decision that’s more complex than just looking at how much revenue they’d raise. But I wanted a sense of perspective that might help to inform some of the broader discussions around taxes, spending, and deficits.

It’s also worth noting that the former prime minister, Keir Starmer, has tied Andy Burnham’s hands because he previously promised that the government wouldn’t touch many of the simple tax levers that I’ll show. 2
Let’s start with income tax. Like many countries, the UK has a progressive income tax system. The first £12,570 that someone earns is not taxed (it’s called a personal allowance). 3
Tax rates then increase with income, often with sharp thresholds. Those on higher incomes don’t just pay more in absolute terms, but also as a share of their income.
The basic tax rate for income up to £50,000 is 20%. This rises to 40% for income between £50,000 and £125,000. And then the top rate for income over £125,000 is 45%. 4
How much extra revenue would the government get if it raised each of those tax rates by one percentage point? You can see this as the green bars in the chart below.
Raising taxes for the top earners would raise an extra £270 million a year. Increasing the basic tax rate, which would hit most earners, would raise just over £8 billion. 30 times as much!
articles.lede: The uncomfortable numbers behind Britain’s largest tax levers.

articles.description: Energy Information Administration - EIA - Official Energy Statistics from the U.S. Government
paragraphs: Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Annual Electric Power Industry Report We estimate that U.S. generation from small-scale or rooftop solar photovoltaic systems (smaller than 1 megawatt of capacity) has increased from 18,812 gigawatthours (GWh) to 92,979 GWh over the last decade. The four states with the highest generation of small-scale solar in the country—California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida—are in regions with more abundant solar resources. Even though it is in a region with lower solar resources, New York ranks as the fifth-largest rooftop solar generation producer as a result of capacity growth supported by technology improvements and state incentives.

The year-over-year change in generation was particularly high in 2022, when total generation grew by 25% compared with the previous year amid record capacity growth. Changes in different programs supporting rooftop solar partly explain this increase in generation. For example, California’s Net Energy Metering (NEM) 2.0 program was available through April 2023. This net metering program offered higher export compensation than the subsequent Net Billing Tariff, or NEM 3.0. All the capacity built under the NEM 2.0 program was grandfathered in, incentivizing higher capacity installation before the current NEM 3.0 took effect.

California accounted for 37% (34,411 GWh) of total U.S. small-scale solar generation in 2025. Between 2024 and 2025, rooftop solar generation in the state grew by 8%, largely due to an increase in capacity. Small-scale solar capacity in California increased from 18 gigawatts in 2024 to 20 gigawatts in 2025.

The state with the next largest amount of small-scale solar power generation is Arizona, accounting for over 6% of total U.S. generation, or 5,795 GWh. Year-over-year generation in Arizona grew only 6% in 2025. The largest increase happened between 2022 and 2023 when generation from small-scale solar grew by 22% in the state. Arizona customers can access a 25% state income-tax credit and other incentives for adding rooftop solar to their properties.

States such as Florida and Texas have seen rapid growth in small-scale solar generation in the last decade as more capacity has been added. Generation in Texas grew from 391 GWh in 2016 to 5,408 GWh last year. Over the same period, Florida’s generation grew from 205 GWh in 2016 to 5,198 GWh in 2025. These two states provide incentives through property tax exemptions and other programs specific to each state and, in some cases, utility.

Programs in states with lower irradiance levels are also supporting growth in rooftop solar generation. New York offers incentives, which have encouraged small-scale solar growth in the state. Other states with similar programs include New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Illinois.
Although generation from small-scale solar continues to grow year over year, the rate of growth has declined since 2022.

EIA uses its surveys of electric utilities to collect information on the number of customers with small-scale solar systems and the aggregated capacity. Electric utilities do not necessarily know how much electricity is generated by rooftop solar on their distribution systems, so generation must be estimated. To develop estimates of generation, we rely on tools such as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory's System Advisor Model and PVWatts. Data on commonly used tilt angles and orientations for small-scale solar systems in California were used as inputs to be representative of tilt angles and orientations in other states.

articles.title: What’s up with Denmark?
articles.description: A conversation with Kristian Jensen of Green Power Denmark.
paragraphs: Industrial symbioses refers to processes wherein the waste products from one industry (say, heat) serve as the inputs to another. If you’re thoughtful about this you can harness some incredible efficiencies, and the Danish are extremely thoughtful about it. I highly recommend one of these tours if you ever get a chance.

While I was in Denmark, I got a chance to interview Kristian Jensen about the Danish energy system. Jensen had a pretty remarkable two-decade stretch in Danish politics, serving at various points as Minister for Foreign Affairs, Minister of Finance, and Minister for Taxation. He now serves as the CEO for Green Power Denmark, the trade association for the country’s big clean-energy industries. (Imagine, my fellow Americans, having a powerful clean-energy trade association. Sigh.)

Jensen is on the center-right, but as you’ll hear, in Denmark that means something dramatically different than it does in the US — he’s a champion of the transition on both environmental and pragmatic grounds. Over the course of an hour we discussed just about every aspect of the country’s energy system, from its district heating systems to the rapid rise of EVs to the widespread use of biomass to the backlash against solar fields. Every time I dig into another country’s energy system and politics I find it more fascinating than I expected, and Denmark was certainly no exception. Enjoy.

David Roberts: I wanted to start with the big picture, the target. Denmark has cut its emissions by around 50% since 1990. It’s a very big deal, very incredible accomplishment, but the target is 70% by 2030.

David Roberts: And the watchdog group, the Independent Climate Council, recently came out and said, basically, “We don’t see the path there. We don’t see that the government has a path there.” The Concito think tank ran a bunch of sort of probabilistic projections recently and put the percentage of hitting that target at about 1%. So I guess the first question is just do you think that target is out of reach?

Kristian Jensen: No, it is not out of reach. It is out of reach if politicians don’t do anything else. So if you have a frozen policy, we should be super optimistic and super lucky if we get to the 70. But the target is not out of reach if you change a few things. For instance, to cut emissions from natural gas powered heat in housing in Denmark and turn that into heat pumps, turn off the gas pipelines to private housing would definitely change something. If we added some more power to the industry and a little less natural gas, a little less oil, we could do something more in these areas.

But if you just have frozen policy from now to 2030, it’s a very slim chance that we’ll get there. When it’s a chance, it’s because Denmark are so focused on wind and solar, that all depends on how the weather will be.

articles.title: Checking back in with Greenlight America
articles.description: A conversation with Matt Traldi.
paragraphs: On this episode, recorded live at Climate Week NYC, I talk with Matt Traldi. He’s the founder and CEO of Greenlight America, which finds the local meetings where clean energy’s fate is being decided and recruits supporters to attend. Traldi argues that siting and permitting approvals turn on who shows up, and that local partners, conservative groups included, outperform outside advocates. We discuss how to measure impact, recent wins and losses, blue-state resistance, data center backlash, and Greenlight’s growth.

Back in January 2025, I introduced Volts listeners to a group called Greenlight America, a nonprofit with a refreshingly simple mission: find the local meetings where the fate of clean energy projects is being determined and make sure that supporters show up to those meetings.

CEO Matt Traldi had about 20 staff then. He said the group had helped advance 4.4 gigawatts of clean energy over the previous year. In 2025, that number reached 20.9 gigawatts. In total, since our last conversation, it’s something like 55.7 gigawatts.

Staff went from 20 to 37, on track for north of 100 by the end of this year. In early 2025 they were involved in four local wins in a quarter; last month, they scored eight in a single day. The model has proven incredibly fruitful.

Traldi shared all this good news when I caught up with him at a Canary Media event during NY Climate Week. We talked about how the group finds local partners, what kinds of messages supporters deliver at these meetings, how it measures success, and how he is navigating such precipitous growth. The conversation was fun and heartening; thanks to Canary for convening it. I hope you enjoy.

David Roberts: Matt, let’s start here. We talked about two years ago on the pod, but maybe some of the audience here, some people listening at home, aren’t familiar yet with the basic model. So maybe just like give the elevator pitch. What is Greenlight? What does it do?

Matt Traldi: Sounds good. First, thank you. Such a pleasure to be back here with you, David. And thank you everyone for being here, everyone listening. So I’m Matt Traldi. I’ll do a quick personal intro and then, you know, go to Greenlight. My background is in political organizing. I was in the labor movement for around a decade. Then in 2016, I was one of the co-founders of Indivisible, a national grassroots network that sprung up to respond to the first time Trump won the election.

And a few years ago, a couple things happened at once. First, my wife and I decided to become parents. I’d always cared about climate, but that pushed it up my personal priority list. And right around the same time while I was at Indivisible, I got to work a little on passing the Inflation Reduction Act and felt very excited and optimistic about this area of work. Still do, by the way. Still do. Spoiler alert.

And so I started learning as much as I could about what it would take to transition the economy to build a ton of clean energy. And what I kept hearing from folks who were doing this work in the industry and the advocacy space was that in the next decade, the overwhelming majority of emissions reduction would come from the power sector, mainly from building big clean energy projects and taking fossil fuels off the grid.

articles.description: How old are leaders across the world, and how long have they been in power?
paragraphs: Paul Biya, Cameroon’s president, is 93 years old. He leads a country where the median age is just 18. A staggering 75-year age gap.

Biya is the most extreme example, but he reflects a pattern we see almost everywhere in the world. Leaders are often a lot older than the populations they govern. Three in four people globally live in a country led by someone over 65. Two in three have a leader older than 70. Most of the world lives under a leader who is past the age when most people retire.

With some help from Claude, I’ve compiled a dataset on the age of each country’s current leader and how long they’ve been in power across more than 140 countries. 1 The leader, here, is the person with the main executive power. This can be the prime minister, president, or monarch. 2

Let’s start with the 19 countries in the G20; it brings together a mix of countries from different regions. Two leaders are over 80: Brazil’s Lula da Silva (who might not be in office for much longer), and Donald Trump. Another seven are in the over-70s camp. Only three — Italy’s Meloni, France’s Macron, and Saudi Arabia’s Mohammed bin Salman — are younger than 50 (if you take King Salman to be Saudi’s executive leader instead, it’s just two).
Vladimir Putin has been in office for 27 years (including four years as prime minister), followed by Turkey’s Erdoğan with 24 years (including eleven as prime minister).
I won’t go through every region one by one, but you can explore each for yourself in the interactive version.
I do want to look at Africa’s distribution, though. It has many leaders who have been ruling for decades.
Cameroon’s president, Paul Biya, is 93 years old and has been in office since he was almost 50. Several are in their eighties and have been leading since their mid-30s.

Of course, many African countries are not democracies, so their leaders have not been kept in office through free and fair elections. 31 of the 41 African countries in this dataset are autocracies, and they’re home to 8 of the 10 continent’s oldest leaders.
The median age — that is, the person in the middle if we lined them all up from youngest to oldest — of leaders globally is around 64 years.

articles.description: Open to all free & paid subscribers.
paragraphs: 1. 🇩🇰 As promised in last month’s note, I flew straight from Climate Week NYC — where I found the sideline conversations quite doomy — to Denmark, where I was immersed in thoughtful, cooperative, successful green infrastructure. It was a balm.
I was on an “Industrial Symbiosis” tour — you can read about it and see the itinerary here.

Copenhagen itself, of course, which is just as dreamy as everyone says — probably my favorite city I’ve ever visited. During every free second I rented one of the many ebikes from one of the many bikeshare services and just rode, rode, rode. I probably put in 200 miles, all of it on safe, grade-separated bike infrastructure, which is ubiquitous. I could go on about this forever but I’ll just say that, although the city is big, every particular spot in it is somehow … cozy. Human-scale. This includes large-scale, dense housing, which is never fronted by busy roads, always tucked away so it feels quiet and intimate. I didn’t take enough pictures (I never remember), but here are a few:

Aarhus, the second largest city in Denmark, is a hidden gem. We visited the port (we visited so many ports …), but my favorite part was our visit to Sydhavnen, the new arts district. They’re developing this raw, post-industrial area between the port and the rest of the city into a district devoted to “creative industries” — artist studios, sound studios, music venues, etc. It is extremely cool. One of the best bits was the recently opened “coal bridge,” adapted from an old rail line that use to carry coal. Modeled on NYC’s Highline, it will connect residential areas to the arts district. Just awesome.

In Skive we got to hang out and talk with the CEO of GreenLab, a semi-off-grid industrial park in the middle of extremely rural land. The park generates most of its own power (~90 percent, as I recall) with wind and solar and uses it to power industrial facilities on the site. There’s a facility that processes agricultural waste into biochar; one that processes plastic waste into chemical feedstocks; one that processes marine byproducts into animal feed; one that electrolyzes hydrogen; and so on. Industrial symbiosis! The extra power goes into batteries and heat batteries, so industries receive steady power and heat around the clock. They’re planning something like a dozen of these parks across the country. I may do a whole pod on it at some point.

The port of Esbjerg (which I heard said aloud probably 100 times and still can not pronounce) — one of Denmark’s newest cities — was cool mainly because it’s become a hub for the offshore wind industry, so we got to see all the giant towers, nacelles, and blades waiting to be loaded on ships. Y’all, that stuff is so big.

We learned about ports, district heating systems, biomass, carbon capture, on and on, but if I had to pull out a central theme, it is this: a society high in social trust can achieve wonders. The drive toward carbon neutrality is supported across the political spectrum. Municipalities own their own electric utilities and district heating systems, so they can make long-term plans and investments, secure in the knowledge that policy won’t lurch in different directions every few years. They conceive of themselves as involved in a common project, as an Us, and it enables an incredible degree of planning and forethought.

articles.description: A conversation with Daniel Palken of Arnold Ventures.
paragraphs: If you are involved in energy discussions, you are almost certainly aware that the long-awaited federal permitting reform bill has finally been unveiled. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) was hashed out over the course of many fraught months of negotiation among Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) of the Environment and Public Works committee and Sens. Mike Lee (R-UT) and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) of the Energy and Natural Resources committee. It is a genuinely bipartisan proposal in that it contains provisions each side loves and provisions each side hates.

The bill is more ambitious than analysts expected, in almost every direction, and it has divided both coalitions. Many climate organizations have urged Democrats in Congress to vote against it, though others have remained neutral or tentatively positive, while clean energy industry boosters and investors love it. Fossil energy groups also love it, though the more radical Freedom Caucus in Congress objects to the presence of virtually any provisions that help renewable energy.
Everyone is fighting over it. Online discussion has been, even for our era, heated and vicious, with personal insults and skepticism about motives flying in every direction.

What I’m going to attempt to do today is have a reasonable discussion of the contents and relative merits of the bill. My guest is Daniel Palken, who runs infrastructure and energy permitting work at Arnold Ventures, a philanthropy devoted to sustainable energy systems. Before that, he spent more than four years in the Senate working for various senators on various bits and pieces of permitting legislation, including 2024’s ill-fated Manchin–Barrasso Energy Permitting Reform Act (EPRA). He has seen the process from the inside and followed the development of all the various provisions closely.

We’re going to discuss how we got here, what the bill actually says, what we might reasonably conclude it will do, and the political considerations going forward. I expect this pod will fully please no one, but I hope that those of you out there who have not tuned in yet will find it, at the very least, educational. Let’s get into it.

articles.description: Ten races will set the rules for 67.4 GW of planned data centers—more capacity than the entire country has operating today
paragraphs: Today we’re publishing The Geography of Compute, our report on where companies are building data centers in the US and why. Today’s story comes from the report’s final section, on the 2026 midterms. If you’re interested in the full report, reach out to learn more about Cleanview’s research subscription. If you’re a journalist, contact us here.

In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown is running ads that call Republican Sen. Jon Husted “the face of data centers in Ohio.” In Michigan, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers backs a one-year moratorium on new data centers. In Texas, both Senate candidates want to end the state’s sales tax break for data centers.
But the near-term future of data centers in America won’t be determined by Congressional midterm elections. Instead, the fate of America’s AI buildout depends on races further down the ballot.

President Trump has made his support for data centers clear. Last month he wrote that towns fighting data centers are choosing to be “backwards and poor.” When Texas’ Governor, Greg Abbott, paused data center approvals in August, Trump called the decision “a mistake.” The President’s support and veto power would make it difficult for Congress to pass any meaningful legislation that regulates data center development.

At the state level, the picture is very different. Governors and state legislators have significant power to block, slow, or otherwise regulate data center development. They can pass moratoriums, strip tax breaks, appoint new utility regulators, and require more stringent environmental and labor standards.
None of these projects have started construction yet, which means the next governor could still decide whether, and on what terms, they get built.

No state with a close governor’s race has more planned data center capacity than Ohio. Developers have announced 21.9 GW of data centers there that haven’t yet broken ground. The Columbus area is already one of the fastest-growing data center markets in the country.

Both candidates for governor say they’d slow that growth down. Republican Vivek Ramaswamy says that on his first day in office, he would “immediately halt the approval of any new data center projects” until his data center law passes. Under his plan, data centers would have to give nearby residents free electricity or compensation and pay full property taxes. Democrat Amy Acton backs a moratorium until data centers pay 100% of their utility costs, among other conditions.

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms wants a temporary statewide pause on new data center construction. “Let us take a pause, assess fully, assess comprehensively, assess the impact that these data centers are having on our environment, on our utility bills,” she said, according to the Georgia Recorder.
Republican Rick Jackson wants to leave the decision to local officials. “Every community should decide,” he has said.

articles.title: Mixed outlook for energy expenditures this winter
articles.description: Energy Information Administration - EIA - Official Energy Statistics from the U.S. Government
paragraphs: Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook We expect energy expenditures this winter to vary because of diverging trends in energy prices among fuels and regional variation in forecast temperatures. We expect that lower prices for natural gas and propane will drive decreases in expenditures this year for the half of U.S. households heating with those fuels. Higher prices for electricity and heating oil drive increased expenditures for households heating with those fuels in our forecast.

Although we expect national average temperatures to be similar to last winter, our forecast assumes warmer temperatures in the Northeast, following a relatively cold winter last year, and much colder temperatures in the West, following an unusually warm winter last year. Temperatures in the Midwest and South are similar to last year.

Homes that use heating oil as their main heating fuel—about 3% of U.S. homes, which are mostly in the Northeast—could see the largest increase in spending this year. We expect a 21% increase in spending on heating oil compared with last winter, driven by increasing global distillate prices. We forecast the price of heating oil will average 34% more this winter than last winter, but warmer forecast temperatures are expected to partly offset our forecast increase in prices. We expect the more than 40% of homes heating with electricity will experience a 4% increase in electricity bills on average. We expect energy expenditures will decrease on average by 9% in homes heating with natural gas and by 3% in those heating with propane.

Global distillate fuel production, which includes heating oil production, has dropped because of reduced global refining activity. Lower production has caused rising international prices, driving up both the cost to import distillate to the United States and the demand for distillate exports from the United States. Through the first seven months of 2026, U.S. distillate exports increased 20% over the same period last year, with much of the increased volumes sent to Europe.

With more costly U.S. imports and higher demand for U.S. exports, U.S. distillate fuel stocks are low heading into winter. We expect inventories will be about 11% below the five-year average in the fourth quarter of 2026.

articles.title: The grueling fight to pass the Inflation Reduction Act
articles.description: A conversation with Leah Stokes.
paragraphs: On September 14, I sat down with Leah Stokes in front of a live audience at Seattle’s Town Hall to talk about her new book, The Carbon Wave. It’s an insider account of how the Inflation Reduction Act got made, braided with the story of the high-risk twin pregnancy she went through while helping to make it. We get into why electrification is the heart of decarbonization, the enduring mystery of what’s going on in Joe Manchin’s head, what it means to trade your carbon footprint for a carbon wave, and how much of the IRA survives. It was followed by questions from the audience.

As listeners know, I tracked the ups and downs of the fight for the Inflation Reduction Act quite closely. Nonetheless, when I read the new book by climate policy scholar and professor Leah Stokes, The Carbon Wave: A Story of Democracy, Parenthood, and the Race to Protect Our Planet, I was turning pages late into the night, in a cold sweat. It might as well have been a thriller.

See, it’s not just about the struggle to write and pass the bill, but about the personal dramas of a few key figures involved, including Stokes herself. During the bill’s two-year gestation, she endured a high-risk pregnancy, bed rest, the premature birth of twins, and 75 days in the NICU. She did media hits from her hospital bed! And that’s only one of the stories in the book.
It does an incredible job of humanizing a story that many people, including us here at Volts, experienced mainly as a wonky battle of models and whitepapers.

Her twins are doing fine today, which is more than one can say about the IRA. The grim Trumpian end to the story is just one of the things I discussed with Stokes at a live book event at Seattle’s Town Hall on September 14. We talked about the bill’s core push for electrification, the enduring mystery of what’s going on in Joe Manchin’s head, and what it means to shift your focus from your carbon footprint to your carbon wave. I hope you enjoy it as much as I did.
